that human life is a struggle of all against all? If the arma-
ments which a nation needs for its own security demand an
ever fresh violation of nature, does not that prove clearly
that this alleged necessity has its origin essentially in sin?
But of course what is necessary and what is sinful are so
closely interwoven in human history that the skein can no
longer be untangled. We are all of us immersed in a complex
structure of life through which the power of evil winds in
multifarious ways, whether we like it or not, and the
individual cannot free himself from the muddle. He can of
course make clear to himself the trend of things, and he
ought not to look on with indifference at the destructive
process which is violating nature; he must attempt to restore
a due respect for nature, and he may be able to do his part
in helping to ensure that the process of ruthless exploitation
is limited to what is strictly essential. But our text does not
draw our attention to the picture of nature in order to
inculcate in us the right attitude towards it, but simply in
order to open our eyes to the real situation with which we
are confronted; nature involved against its will in the history
of man and therefore subjected to the curse of ravage and
destruction. We notice what she might and ought to be and
what she is ever less and less. As we grow aware of these
things we feel a sense of horror creeping over us, and we
gain some surmise of the tragic doom which weighs upon
our world, of the extent to which our life has become
entangled in evil, and there arises in us a longing and a
sighing for release and redemption.
II
This survey of the world of nature, disturbed and defaced
by human history, should bring us to consider the drama of
human life. Is the life of a man as it should be? Is it not also
distorted and corrupted? To what has the course of history
led us? Do we not to-day perceive the world tremble and
